name: Escitalopram
summary: A first-line choice for panic. Start at 5 mg, half the usual depression dose, because panic makes people unusually sensitive to early overstimulation.

name: Escitalopram
summary: A first-line choice for generalized anxiety, with placebo-controlled trial support and few drug interactions.

name: Sertraline
summary: A first-line choice for panic. Start at 25 mg and titrate slowly; more diarrhea and early agitation than most SSRIs.

name: Sertraline
summary: A first-line choice for generalized anxiety, with the most reassuring pregnancy data and very few interactions.

name: Paroxetine
summary: Effective for panic and mildly sedating, which some people prefer early on. Withdrawal is difficult without a slow taper.

name: Paroxetine
summary: The most extensively trialled SSRI for generalized anxiety. Weight gain, sexual side effects, and withdrawal are the main drawbacks.

name: Fluoxetine
summary: Effective for panic but activating, so start at 5 mg. The long half-life means missed doses and stopping are far more forgiving.

name: Fluoxetine
summary: Widely used for generalized anxiety on the strength of open trials and practice rather than placebo-controlled trials.

name: Citalopram
summary: Effective for panic with few interactions. Doses above 40 mg, or 20 mg over age 60, raise QT-interval concerns.

name: Citalopram
summary: Effective for generalized anxiety with few interactions, but more weight gain than fluoxetine and a dose ceiling for QT.

name: Fluvoxamine
summary: Trial-proven for panic and less activating than most SSRIs, but it inhibits CYP1A2 and 2C19 and interacts widely.

name: Fluvoxamine
summary: Used for generalized anxiety mostly by extension from other anxiety disorders. Significant drug interactions.

name: Venlafaxine ER
summary: The usual next step after two SSRIs fail in panic. Use the extended-release form only; monitor blood pressure at every visit.

name: Venlafaxine ER
summary: A first-line option for generalized anxiety with efficacy shown out to six months. Blood pressure rises at higher doses.

name: Duloxetine
summary: Not typically used for panic; there are no randomized trials and very few open-label studies in this condition.

name: Duloxetine
summary: A first-line option for generalized anxiety, and the usual pick when sexual side effects are the main worry.

name: Buspirone
summary: Randomized trials have not supported buspirone for panic disorder. Consider it only if the diagnosis is in question.

name: Buspirone
summary: The preferred add-on for a partial response in generalized anxiety. No dependence or withdrawal, but slow onset and modest effect.

name: Gabapentin
summary: Used alongside an SSRI for early distress when a benzodiazepine is unwise, especially with a substance use history. Works within days.

name: Gabapentin
summary: A reasonable third-line option in generalized anxiety and the preferred bridge in people with a substance use history.

name: Pregabalin
summary: An alternative to gabapentin with a similar profile. Schedule V in the US and more misuse concern.

name: Pregabalin
summary: Approved for anxiety outside the US and effective in trials. Most people need above 150 mg/day. Sedation and dizziness are common.

name: Mirtazapine
summary: Used as an add-on for panic with insomnia, on the strength of case reports and open trials rather than randomized data.

name: Mirtazapine
summary: An option for generalized anxiety with prominent insomnia. Trial evidence is thin; sedation and appetite are the trade-off.

name: Hydroxyzine
summary: Not studied in panic disorder. Its sedation may blunt an attack but it does not treat the underlying condition.

name: Hydroxyzine
summary: Works within an hour and carries no dependence risk, so it is the usual bridge when a benzodiazepine is off the table. Meta-analysis quality is poor.

name: Vilazodone
summary: No randomized trials in panic disorder.

name: Vilazodone
summary: As effective as other serotonin reuptake inhibitors in generalized anxiety, with possibly less sexual dysfunction and more nausea.

name: Clonazepam
summary: FDA-approved for panic and effective within the first week. Reserved for early distress or partial response, then tapered over 10 to 12 weeks.

name: Clonazepam
summary: Effective and fast, but held back until other options are exhausted because of dependence, falls, and cognitive effects.

name: Lorazepam
summary: Effective in trials and fast, but the short half-life brings interdose rebound and a harder taper than clonazepam. Best kept for as-needed use or a short bridge.

name: Lorazepam
summary: The suggested short-term cover for early SSRI agitation and insomnia at 1 to 2 mg a day, then tapered by 25 percent a week. Not a long-term answer.

name: Imipramine
summary: Sixteen trials support tricyclics for panic, though most used imipramine while nortriptyline is better tolerated. Cardiotoxic in overdose.

name: Imipramine
summary: Effective for generalized anxiety, including without comorbid depression, but reserved because of overdose risk and tolerability.

name: Quetiapine
summary: A controlled augmentation trial in SSRI-resistant panic found no benefit over placebo.

name: Quetiapine
summary: Randomized trials support it for refractory generalized anxiety, but metabolic effects, sedation, and tardive dyskinesia keep it last.

name: Propranolol
summary: Trials have not found beta blockers effective for panic disorder. It blunts palpitations and tremor without touching the fear that drives them.

name: Propranolol
summary: Weak evidence as a daily treatment for generalized anxiety, but a single dose before a specific event is where it earns its place.
